title: AML Agents Briefing — Monday, 03 August 2026
script:
ALEX: Welcome to AML Agents Briefing for Sunday the third of August 2026. This is your audio overview of the most material AML and financial crime developments across Asia-Pacific today. Full detail, the obligation register, news sources, and horizon scanning are all at amlagents dot streamlit dot app.

JORDAN: Big day, Alex. We've got a stablecoin settlement development with real compliance implications, a fraud warning out of Singapore that MLROs should share with their teams today, and some upcoming obligations listeners need to have on their radar right now.

ALEX: Let's start with the stablecoin story, because this one has a direct read-across for transaction monitoring and settlement-layer risk. Partior and OpenAssets have completed a proof of concept demonstrating atomic delivery-versus-payment settlement across digital assets, regulated stablecoins, and commercial tokenised deposits. Atomic settlement means both legs of a transaction complete simultaneously, with no daylight exposure. That's a significant capability shift.

JORDAN: So Alex, what does this actually mean for how institutions structure their AML controls? Because if settlement is instantaneous, the window for intervention effectively closes.

ALEX: Exactly right. In a traditional settlement model, there's a lag between instruction and finality. That lag is where your transaction monitoring, sanctions screening, and pre-settlement review processes sit. Atomic settlement compresses that window to near zero. The compliance infrastructure needs to move upstream, into onboarding, wallet attribution, and pre-transaction screening rather than post-transaction review.

JORDAN: So the action for listeners here is fairly clear. If you're the MLRO or head of financial crime compliance at a bank, exchange, or payment institution that is piloting tokenised assets or stablecoins, you need to convene your transaction monitoring team this week and stress-test whether your current controls can operate at the pre-settlement layer. If your KYT vendor, that's know-your-transaction, is only covering post-settlement flows, you likely have a gap. Raise that with your technology and product teams before any live deployment.

ALEX: Moving on, and this one is directly relevant to Singapore-based compliance teams. The Institute of Banking and Finance and the Monetary Authority of Singapore issued a joint public warning on the third of August against a fraudulent training programme impersonating both institutions. The fake course advertised a three-day Capital Markets and Financial Advisory Services examination preparation programme at a fee of four hundred and ninety Singapore dollars.

JORDAN: This is a social engineering threat, but it's also a governance issue. Employees are the target here.

ALEX: Right. Fraudsters are using the IBF and MAS brand names to lend credibility. The risk is that junior compliance staff or new joiners, who are precisely the people likely to be seeking regulated qualifications, are the most exposed. So what should listeners do?

JORDAN: Two things. First, circulate the MAS and IBF warning to your team today, particularly to staff in Singapore who are in active CPD or licensing cycles. Second, use this as a prompt to review your firm's staff guidance on verifying training providers. Your employees should always confirm course registration directly through the IBF's official portal or the MAS website before making any payment. If you haven't issued that guidance in the last twelve months, issue it this week.

ALEX: Shifting to obligations, and there are three coming up that warrant attention. The first is Australia, where AUSTRAC's annual compliance report under Part 13 of the AML and CTF Rules should already have been lodged for the calendar year 2024 reporting period. The deadline was the thirty-first of March 2025. If there are any reporting entities in your group that missed that, late lodgement attracts daily civil penalties and a misleading attestation can carry criminal liability under Section 137 of the relevant Act. The second is Indonesia, where POJK 12 requires the annual independent review of the AML and CFT programme to have been completed by the thirtieth of June 2025, with findings presented to the Risk Oversight Committee and the Board of Commissioners. And the third is Hong Kong, where the HKMA's AML and CFT Guideline, Section 11, requires the annual self-assessment return for calendar year 2024 to be submitted by the thirtieth of September 2025.

JORDAN: For listeners with entities across these jurisdictions, the Hong Kong return is the most immediately actionable. That September deadline is live. Pull your HKMA self-assessment template now, confirm Internal Audit has signed off on the independent validation, and make sure the completed Excel submission is queued for your Relationship Manager at the HKMA. Don't leave it to the final week of September.

ALEX: On what to watch, the horizon scanning feed has three items worth flagging. AUSTRAC published Tranche 2 guidance for legal practitioners covering customer engagement triggers, source-of-wealth diligence in conveyancing, and how the legal professional privilege carve-out interacts with suspicious matter reporting obligations. Bank Negara Malaysia published a typology bulletin on investment scams routed through digital banks and crypto exchanges, with mule-account indicators including rapid post-onboarding velocity spikes and inbound transfers from multiple unrelated retail senders. And AUSTRAC announced a forty-seven million Australian dollar civil penalty against a major registered digital currency exchange for systemic failures in transaction monitoring, mule detection, and suspicious matter report timeliness.

JORDAN: Three actions for this week. For Australian reporting entities with any exposure to Tranche 2 obligations, add the AUSTRAC legal practitioner guidance to your next thematic review scope and check whether your customer engagement triggers are aligned with the new guidance. For compliance teams in Malaysia with digital bank or crypto exposure, pull the BNM typology bulletin and run it against your current mule-account detection scenarios. And for digital currency exchange compliance leads anywhere in the region, the AUSTRAC enforcement action is the clearest possible signal: review your SMR timeliness metrics and your mule detection logic before your next regulator touchpoint.

JORDAN: That's your briefing for today. Head to amlagents dot streamlit dot app for the full obligation register, underlying sources, and the complete horizon-scanning feed.

ALEX: Thanks for listening. We'll be back with the next update. Stay sharp out there.
